concept.body: CPCTC = Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent. It runs in ONE direction: congruent triangles ⇒ every pair of corresponding parts is equal. It is the LAST move in a proof — you must prove the triangles congruent (by a criterion) BEFORE you may extract parts with it.

explanationVariants: CPCTC comes AFTER a congruence is proven — it reads parts out of it.

widget.prompt: In a proof, CPCTC is used…

options.label: after proving the triangles congruent
options.feedback: CPCTC extracts equal parts from an established congruence, so it comes last.

options.label: before choosing a criterion
options.feedback: There's no congruence to draw from yet — prove it with a criterion first, then CPCTC.

options.label: instead of a criterion
options.feedback: CPCTC doesn't PROVE congruence; it uses one. You still need a criterion first.

options.label: only in similarity proofs
options.feedback: CPCTC is about CONGRUENT triangles and equal parts — not similarity.

steps.body: Now put criteria to work. A congruence proof has two acts: FIRST prove the triangles congruent by a criterion (SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS); THEN, because congruent triangles match in every part, read off whatever equal side or angle you need. That second act has a name: **CPCTC** — Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent.

widget.prompt: AB = CB, so the legs are locked equal at 6. Drag the apex angle to 50° and watch the two base angles the whole way — can you ever make ∠A and ∠C disagree?
widget.constraintFeedback: You released the lock, so the legs are no longer equal — the base angles are now reading a different triangle than the one the proof is about. Re-lock them.
widget.successFeedback: They never disagree. With AB = CB and D the midpoint of AC, the two halves share three pairs of equal sides — SSS — so △ABD ≅ △CBD, and ∠A = ∠C follows by CPCTC. The lab shows the conclusion is forced at every apex angle, not just this one.
widget.criterionFeedback: SSA does not lock a triangle. The proof uses three pairs of equal SIDES: AB = CB, the shared BD, and AD = DC from the midpoint.
widget.angleFeedback: Right criterion — now bring the apex angle to 50°.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Drag through several apex angles before checking. The claim is that ∠A = ∠C ALWAYS, which one position cannot show.

explanationVariants: CPCTC is valid only AFTER the triangles are proven congruent — it reads parts OUT of an established congruence.
First earn the congruence (by a criterion); only then does CPCTC hand you the equal parts.

widget.prompt: At what point in a proof may you use CPCTC?

options.label: only after the triangles have been proven congruent
options.feedback: CPCTC extracts equal parts FROM a congruence — so the congruence must be established first.

options.label: as the very first step, to get started
options.feedback: CPCTC needs a congruence to draw from — it can't come before one exists. Prove congruence first.

options.label: any time two triangles share a side
options.feedback: A shared side alone isn't congruence. You must first prove the triangles congruent by a criterion.

options.label: only when using SSS
options.feedback: CPCTC follows ANY criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS) — not just SSS. It just needs an established congruence.

steps.body: Choosing the criterion is a matching game: inventory what you're GIVEN (and what's free — shared sides are reflexive, vertical angles are equal), then pick the criterion whose pattern you can complete. Given two sides and the angle between? SAS. Two angles and a side? ASA or AAS. Three sides? SSS.

widget.prompt: Two triangles share a side. You're also given a pair of equal angles at each end of that shared side. Which criterion fits?

options.label: ASA: angles with their included side
options.feedback: Two angles with the side BETWEEN them — and the shared side is reflexively equal. That's ASA.

options.label: SSS: three equal side pairs
options.feedback: You're given angles, not three sides. Only one side (the shared one) is known equal — SSS needs three.

options.label: SAS: two equal sides and an angle
options.feedback: SAS needs two SIDES with the included angle. Here you have two ANGLES with the included side — that's ASA.

options.label: SSA: two equal sides and an angle
options.feedback: SSA isn't a valid criterion at all — and you have angles at both ends of the side, which is the ASA pattern.

explanationVariants: By CPCTC corresponding sides are equal, so the partner of a length-15 side is also 15.
Once congruent, matching parts share measures — the corresponding side is 15.

widget.prompt: △ABC ≅ △DEF has been proven. If AB = 15, what is DE?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 doubles it — but congruent triangles are the SAME size. Corresponding sides are EQUAL: DE = AB = 15.
7.5 halves it — congruence preserves size exactly. DE corresponds to AB, so DE = 15.

steps.body: One caution graders love: **letter order encodes correspondence.** In △ABC ≅ △DEF, A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. So AB corresponds to DE — not to EF. When you apply CPCTC, match parts by POSITION in the statement, never by how the triangle happens to look.

options.label: TU
options.feedback: Q↔T and R↔U (positions 2 and 3), so QR corresponds to TU.

options.label: ST
options.feedback: ST is positions 1–2, corresponding to PQ. QR is positions 2–3: TU.

options.label: SU
options.feedback: SU is positions 1–3, corresponding to PR. QR (positions 2–3) matches TU.

options.label: PR
options.feedback: PR is a side of the SAME triangle as QR — correspondence pairs across the two triangles.

hints: Inventory: two given equal sides, plus what's free at the shared vertex?
Vertical angles at the crossing are equal — that's the included angle between the two given sides.
Two sides + the included (vertical) angle = SAS; then CPCTC finishes.
explanationVariants: The two given sides meet at the crossing, where vertical angles are equal — that included angle gives SAS congruence, and CPCTC then yields the required equal parts.
Vertical angles supply the included angle between the two equal sides: SAS, then CPCTC.

widget.prompt: Segments AC and BD cross at P, with AP = CP and BP = DP. To prove △APB ≅ △CPD, which criterion applies?

options.label: SAS: sides with their included angle
options.feedback: AP = CP and BP = DP are the two sides; ∠APB = ∠CPD are vertical (equal) — the included angle. That's SAS.

options.label: SSS: three equal side pairs
options.feedback: Only two side pairs are given (AP=CP, BP=DP); the third sides aren't known equal. Use the vertical angle instead: SAS.

options.label: ASA: angles with included side
options.feedback: Only ONE angle pair is known (the vertical angles). ASA needs two — here you pair it with two sides: SAS.

options.label: AAS: angles with nonincluded side
options.feedback: AAS needs TWO angle pairs; you have one angle pair and two sides. The included vertical angle makes it SAS.

takeaways: A congruence proof: first a criterion (SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS), then CPCTC for the parts.
CPCTC is valid only AFTER congruence is established.
Match corresponding parts by letter POSITION, not by the picture.
